sentence: 19-year-old male patient referred from a regional hospital for surgery for hydrocephalus.
He had a history of approximately 1 year of left hemicranial headache that worsened with exertion.
In recent weeks the headache has increased in intensity and frequency.
The neurological examination showed only bilateral papilledema.

The patient provided a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showing supratentorial ventricular dilation with an Evans index of 0.43, periependymal clearance in the frontal horns, and a small tectal lesion that was not modified with contrast.
With the diagnosis of stenosis of the Sylvian aqueduct, an endoscopic premammillary ventriculocisternostomy was performed through a right frontal burr hole according to the usual technique3.
A Mayfield head (Ohio Medical Instrument Co, Inc., Cincinnati, OH, USA) was used to immobilize the head.
The immediate postoperative period passed without incident although the patient suffered from headache.

48 hours after surgery and prior to scheduled hospital discharge, a new MRI was performed in which the presence of an epidural hematoma located in the left parietal area with mass effect on the ipsilateral lateral ventricle was striking.
A left parietal craniotomy was then performed, observing that there was a perforation that crossed the entire bone without affecting the dura mater.
The hematoma was drained and a small bleeding dural artery was coagulated.
The patient was discharged after 6 days with only a certain degree of headache.
One year after surgery he is asymptomatic and the tectal lesion shows no changes in MRI studies.
